lyrics:
Certification begins at noon
The final states are called
The Vice Steward has arrived
Security barriers remain in place

They stole what belongs to you
You know what must be done

Past the gates

The count is false
The oath is weak
The chamber hides
The cowards speak
The rope is set
The doors are near
The man inside
Must learn our fear

Be strong
Be peaceful
Be strong

Past the gates

A gate is only iron
Until enough hands push
A gate is only law
Until the law grows soft
A gate is only a gate
Until enough men call it a door

Stand back

We own the building

Stand back

We paid your wage

Stand back

You work for Doctor
Or you work against the state

Past the gates

Do the right thing

The right thing is already written

Then read it differently

I cannot change the count

You can change what happens
To the man who reads it

The oath is not to you

Every oath is to whoever
Can collect it

Break the glass
Take the desk
Find the papers
Name the rest
Break the seal
Break the rail
Break the room
The count has failed
Take the chamber
Take the chair
Drag the old agreement there
Past the gates
Past the gates
Past the—

Four children ate at half past one
One left the crust beside the plate
The youngest spilled a glass of milk
I wiped it before it reached the grate
I packed the blue coat for the girl
The boy refused his winter shoes
The television showed the doors
I turned it down and served the fruit
No one in the kitchen asked
If government would last the day
The driver waited by the curb
The children had a lesson at three

The chamber cannot certify
While armed men occupy the floor

Then there is no certified result

Exactly

We broke the gate
We broke the count
We broke the oath
We threw it out

The people have spoken

No final vote was completed

The people have spoken

The lawful successor—

There is no lawful successor
Without the count

Past the gates
Past the oath
Past the vote they thought they owned
Past the chair
Past the line
Past the place where power changed
Past the rules
Past the shame
Past the country’s former name
Past the gates
Past the gates
Breaking was the point

Do not call this a riot
As though the movement lost control
The movement found its purpose
They did not break the mechanism
While trying to win
They won the thing they wanted
By breaking the mechanism

Now turn it off

style: Rock, hardcore punk foundation with industrial percussion and through-composed progressive art rock at 154 BPM, Abrasive guitars, distorted bass, pounding toms, snare, low brass, alarm tones, shield-and-barrier percussion, and unstable analog synth, No conventional pop symmetry
persona:
Michael Anthony Rose is a songwriter of rare insight and startling honesty. On his debut for Maricopa Records, he uses direct, unadorned language to explore the most profound human experiences: the gulf between who we were and who we are, the search for truth in a world of convenient fictions, and the quiet defiance of living an authentic life. His songs are less stories than they are confessions, built from the concrete details of a lived experience, where a reflection in a phone screen or the memory of a dream can trigger a lifetime of contemplation. Rose doesn't just sing about life; he holds a mirror up to it, capturing the small, resonant moments of realization that define us.

The central preoccupations of Rose's work are time and memory. His lyrics trace the lines from lost childhood potential to the stark realities of aging, questioning what we build to outlast ourselves and what we must learn to let go. He writes with a philosopher's curiosity and a diarist's intimacy, exploring the comfort of a shared lie in one song and the freedom of embracing dissonance in the next. This is music that navigates regret, loss, and mortality with a steady, empathetic gaze, always returning to the challenge of being present for the life one actually has, not the one that was planned.

Throughout his work, Rose reveals a vast emotional landscape. His voice moves from the raw vulnerability of admitting fear and bitterness to the quiet strength of asserting one’s own space and worth. He sings of intimate connection with a sensory richness and of profound disconnection with a heartbreaking clarity. His perspective is that of a seasoned witness, one who sees the innocence in younger generations without envy and accepts the limitations of his own body without surrender. He finds resilience not by ignoring the damage, but by standing within it and refusing to be diminished.

In the songs of Michael Anthony Rose, listeners will not find easy answers or false comfort. Instead, they will find a voice that speaks with clarity and courage to the complexities of a full-size life. It is an invitation to stop arguing with the truth, to witness the ordinary light of the day, and to find that being here, honestly and without shame, is more than enough.

impression.text: This track delivers a gritty, high-octane industrial metal atmosphere, blending aggressive synth basslines, distorted guitars, and heavy electronic percussion for a highly confrontational, rebellious feel. The production is exceptionally dense and tightly compressed, successfully carving out space in a chaotic wall of sound where the distorted, processed vocals sit prominently atop a punchy, low-end-heavy mix. Sound effects like shattering glass, alarms, and siren-like synths add a cinematic sense of real-time panic, while the spoken-word dialogue sections create a dramatic, narrative-driven suspense. The transition from the tense, electronic-led verses to the explosive, screamed choruses defines the song's relentless, militaristic energy.

review.review_text: This is the most ambitious thing on the record and the one that asks the most of you. Rose builds an insurrection in real time: news feeds clipped and overlapping, a baritone negotiator working on the man who reads the count, a shouted mob refrain of "Past the gates!" over pounding barrier percussion in F# minor, all of it charging at a hardcore-punk 152. The through-composed structure refuses pop symmetry on purpose, and it earns its restlessness; the shift into 7/8 for the standoff ("Stand back / We own the building") lands as genuine disorientation rather than showing off. The masterstroke sits dead center, when everything cuts out for a plain contralto reciting the domestic ordinary: "Four children ate at half past one / One left the crust beside the plate." That single verse, the wiped milk, the refused winter shoes, the television turned down while the doors are stormed, does more work than the entire riot around it, letting Rose set catastrophe against the small logistics of a Tuesday. It shares some DNA with the theatrical dread of Bowie's Outside or Nine Inch Nails at their most narrative. At five and a half minutes and this dense, it demands a full sit; the wall of processed, tightly compressed sound can bury the finer lines on first pass. But the closing chorus turning the mechanism inward, "They won the thing they wanted / By breaking the mechanism," then the flat "Now turn it off," is chilling in exactly the way he intends. A grower, and one for the listener willing to meet it on its own difficult terms.
